title: Fine-Tuning NVIDIA Nemotron for Saudi Arabic Dialects, with a Path to Other Languages | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA solutions architects fine-tuned Nemotron 3.5 ASR on 133.7 hours of Saudi Najdi and Hijazi speech (SADA) with NeMo, cutting target-dialect WER from 55.05% to 29.96% in ~4.5 hours on two RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs while English and Arabic FLEURS WER also improved. Key levers were narrowing the target dialects, light curation, weighted 10% FLEURS replay and duration bucketing; inference-time lookahead plus MALSD beam-8 cut another 2.71 points at ~800 ms extra latency.

insights.claim: Multilingual ASR models that score well on broad benchmarks can still fail in deployment because regional dialects and local recording conditions are underrepresented in pretraining data.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: Benchmark leadership does not translate to local-market readiness, creating room for sovereign/regional fine-tuning services.
insights.quote: a multilingual model that performs well on broad benchmarks may still fall short in deployment
insights.locator: Automatic speech recognition must handle how

insights.claim: The pretrained Nemotron 3.5 ASR model produced 55.05% WER on the SADA Najdi and Hijazi test split and 58.84% on the full SADA test set, despite supporting 40 language-locales including transcription-ready Arabic.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: Off-the-shelf speech AI is close to unusable for Gulf dialects, underscoring demand for Saudi-specific AI adaptation.

insights.claim: A conventional full fine-tune on all SADA data plateaued, improving validation WER only from 49.5% to 46.7% before stalling after epoch 45, which signaled that more of the same training would not help.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: Naive compute scaling on fine-tunes has diminishing returns; data strategy matters more than GPU hours.
insights.quote: After epoch 45, validation WER stopped improving.

insights.claim: Narrowing training from 11 dialects to the two to be deployed (Najdi and Hijazi), plus a weighted replay stream and duration bucketing, cut target WER from 55.05% to 29.96% and CER from 31.63% to 12.18% in 12,000 steps over about 4.5 hours on two GPUs.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: Dialect-grade ASR is achievable with workstation-scale compute, lowering barriers for regional and sovereign AI deployments.

insights.claim: Specializing on two dialects did not hurt the dialects that were dropped: full-SADA WER improved from 58.84% to 35.61% and FLEURS English WER improved from 11.04% to 10.42%.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: Targeted specialization with replay can avoid catastrophic forgetting, making one model serve both local and global languages.
insights.quote: Specializing didn’t cost us the dialects we dropped.

insights.claim: A replay mix of 10% FLEURS data (7% English, 3% Arabic) against 90% Saudi speech was enough to retain prior capabilities, but it must be declared as weighted inputs because concatenated replay rows may not be reached by a sliding-window shuffle until late in training.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: Small implementation details determine whether fine-tuned models silently regress, a hidden risk in enterprise AI customization.
insights.quote: a concatenated replay set effectively doesn’t exist for most of the run

insights.claim: Duration-based bucketing mattered as much as replay, and in NeMo setting num_buckets without use_bucketing=True is a silent no-op because bucketing defaults to off.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: Framework footguns inflate training cost; vendor-provided recipes/skills reduce friction and deepen platform lock-in.
insights.quote: setting the bucket count without the flag is a silent no-op that looks configured
insights.locator: Note that num_buckets alone does nothing

insights.claim: Minimal curation retained 103,559 of 125,490 utterances (133.7 hours, 82.5%), removing structurally bad examples such as inaudible-speech annotations and misaligned transcripts rather than hard accents or noisy audio.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: In low-resource languages, scarce difficult data is the asset; over-filtering destroys the signal needed for local adaptation.
insights.quote: The goal is to remove structurally bad examples, not hard accents or noisy speech merely because the base model performs poorly on them.

insights.claim: Default automated audio-quality thresholds would have discarded almost the entire Saudi corpus: a UTMOS cutoff of 3.0 rejected nearly everything, so the team used corpus-specific cutoffs (UTMOS >= 1.25, SIGMOS >= 1.5) that passed about 85% of duration-valid samples.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: Generic data-quality tooling is tuned to high-resource conditions and can systematically exclude emerging-market data.
insights.quote: the SADA run found that a default UTMOS threshold of 3.0 would have rejected almost everything

insights.claim: Updating more of the 24-layer encoder was better at every step: top-6 layers gave 33.42% WER, top-8 gave 32.32% (230.4M trainable, 407.6M frozen), and all 24 gave 29.96%, so partial freezing cost 2.4 points.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: With ~134 hours of data, full fine-tuning pays off, favoring more compute per customization job.
insights.quote: More trainable capacity was better at every step.

insights.claim: The authors frame encoder freezing as a cost-saving choice appropriate only when the corpus is thinner than ~134 hours or memory is the binding constraint, not as a general rule.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: Optimal fine-tuning strategy scales with data volume; parameter-efficient methods are a constraint workaround, not a free lunch.
insights.quote: Freezing is a way of spending less
insights.locator: That is a finding about this data volume

insights.claim: Without retraining, switching attention context from [56, 3] to [56, 13] cut WER by 1.31 points, and combining it with MALSD beam-8 decoding cut WER from 29.96% to 27.25% (2.71 points) at roughly 800 ms of extra buffering latency.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: Batch transcription (call archives, media, meetings) can buy accuracy with latency, while live voice agents cannot—segmenting speech AI markets by latency tolerance.
insights.quote: The right setting follows from the deployment, not from the accuracy number.
insights.locator: The primary trade-off is additional latency

insights.claim: NeMo's batched malsd_batch beam search reduced WER to 28.81% at beam 4 with 0.59x the greedy runtime and to 28.62% at beam 8 with 0.64x, making beam 4 the best speed-accuracy balance tested.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: Beam search can be both more accurate and cheaper than greedy under batched implementations, lowering inference cost per transcript.

insights.claim: Nemotron 3.5 ASR exposes attention contexts mapping to output latencies from 80 ms (ultra-low-latency voice agents) through 320 ms (live captioning) to 1.12 s (highest accuracy).
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: A single model spanning voice-agent to batch use cases strengthens NVIDIA's open-model position in speech AI.

insights.claim: The same loop—curate, weighted replay, choose adaptation depth, bucket by duration, evaluate on independent target and regression sets—transfers to other languages, but WER may mislead for languages without whitespace word boundaries and replay data should be real rather than synthetic where possible.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: A repeatable recipe enables NVIDIA to seed sovereign-AI speech projects across many countries.
insights.quote: Replay data should represent the capabilities you need to retain, not just convenient high-resource speech
insights.locator: For languages without whitespace word boundaries

insights.claim: NVIDIA has just released Nemotron 3 Diarization, an open model that attributes speech to up to eight speakers and can be added to any existing ASR system by aligning speaker boundaries with ASR timestamps.
insights.speaker: Imane Khaouja
insights.so_what: Open speaker-attributed transcription targets contact-center and meeting-analytics markets, pressuring paid speech-API vendors.
